pages.x: After the disaster of the Great Leap Forward, Mao felt pushed aside by party leaders like Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping. In 1966, aged 72, he called on China's young people to rise against the party's own leaders, whom he accused of taking the capitalist road. To show he was still strong, he swam in the Yangtze.

Millions of students formed Red Guard units and, waving Mao's Little Red Book, poured into Beijing for huge rallies in Tiananmen Square. They set out to smash the four olds, old customs, culture, habits and ideas: they burned books, wrecked temples and smashed antiques.

Teachers, writers, officials and anyone from a bad class background were dragged before jeering crowds, beaten, paraded in dunce's caps and sent to prison or labour camps. Many were killed or took their own lives. Rival Red Guard groups fought each other with guns, until the army stepped in.

Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, was beaten, denied medicine and died in prison in 1969. Deng Xiaoping was sent to work in a tractor factory, and his son was left paralysed after a fall from a window while held by Red Guards. Some 17 million young people were sent to the countryside to learn from the peasants.

pages.t: The last flight of Lin Biao
pages.x: Mao's chosen heir, Marshal Lin Biao, who had spread the cult of the Little Red Book, was accused of plotting against him. In September 1971 Lin fled with his family by plane, and it crashed in Mongolia, killing everyone on board. What really happened is still a mystery.

Mao died in September 1976. Within a month his widow, Jiang Qing, and three allies, the Gang of Four, were arrested and blamed for the chaos. Deng Xiaoping came back to power and began the reforms that opened China to the world.

The Communist Party later called the Cultural Revolution a catastrophe, but it is still a touchy subject in China and little taught in schools. A whole generation lost its education, and countless temples, books and works of art were destroyed. Its memory shaped Deng's turn to calm, practical reform.
